===Etymology 1===
{{ety|en|id=flying mammal}}
[[File:Mariana_Fruit_Bat.jpg|thumb|upright|Mariana's fruit '''bat''' ({{taxlink|Pteropus mariannus|species}}) ({{senseno|en|Q28425}})]]

Variant of {{inh|en|enm|bakke}}, of {{der|en|gmq}} origin (akin to {{cog|da|aftenbakke}} and {{cog|sv|nattbacka}}, both now dialectal). Swedish also has {{m|sv|nattblacka}}, and Icelandic has {{m|is|leðurblaka}}, in which the second element is a derivative of {{m|non|blaka||to flap}}, but it is unclear whether this word is also the source of ''bakke'', ''backa'', etc.

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# {{senseid|en|Q28425}} Any flying [[mammal]] of the order {{taxfmt|Chiroptera|order}}, usually small and [[nocturnal]], [[insectivorous]] or [[frugivorous]].
#: {{syn|en|chiropter|chiropteran|flindermouse|flitterbat|flittermouse|fluttermouse|flying mouse|rattlemouse|reremouse}}
#* {{RQ:Rinehart Hopwood Bat|I|01|passage=The Bat—they called him the Bat. Like a '''bat''' he chose the night hours for his work of rapine; like a '''bat''' he struck and vanished, pouncingly, noiselessly; like a '''bat''' he never showed himself to the face of the day.}}
#* '''2012''', Suemedha Sood, {{monospace|(bbc.co.uk)}} [https://web.archive.org/web/20120213011349/http://www.bbc.com/travel/blog/20120209-travelwise-texas-love-bats Travelwise: Texas love bats] [sic]
#*: As well as being worth millions of dollars to the Texan agriculture industry, these mammals are worth millions of dollars to the state’s tourism industry. Texas is home to the world’s largest known '''bat''' colony (in Comal County), and the world’s largest urban '''bat''' colony (in Austin). '''Bat''' watching is a common activity, with the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department offering more '''bat'''-viewing sites than anywhere else in the US.
# {{senseid|en|old woman, derogatorily}} {{lb|en|derogatory}} An old woman.
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2000|author=w:Bill Oddie|title=Gripping Yarns|page=196|passage="Isn't it lovely?" I smiled and thought: "Yes it is. It's also a Blackbird, you silly old '''bat'''!}}

===Etymology 2===
[[File:Marcus_Thames_Tigers_2007.jpg|thumb|A player swinging a baseball '''bat''' ({{senseno|en|club}})]]

{{ety|en|id=club|:inh|enm:bat<id:club>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|bat,batte}}, from {{inh|en|ang|batt||bat, club, cudgel}}, probably of {{der|en|cel}} origin, compare {{cog|obt|bath||club, cudgel}} and modern {{cog|br|bazh||swagger stick}}, ultimately from a derivative of {{der|en|ine-pro|*bʰedʰh₂-||to strike, beat, pierce}}, similar to the Gaulish source of {{cog|la|battuō||to beat, pound}}.<ref>Beekes, R. S. P. (1997). Sound Law and Analogy: Papers in Honor of Robert S.P. Beekes on the Occasion of His 60th Birthday. Netherlands: Rodopi, p. 312</ref>

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# A [[club]], made of wood like a [[baseball]] bat or otherwise, used as a [[weapon]]
# {{senseid|en|club}} A [[club]] made of wood or aluminium used for striking the ball in sports such as [[baseball]], [[softball]] and [[cricket]].
# A [[turn]] at [[hitting]] the [[ball]] with a bat in a [[game]].
#: {{ux|en|You've been in for ages. Can I have a '''bat''' now?}}
# A player rated according to skill in batting.
#: {{ux|en|He's a good fielder and a valuable '''bat'''.}}
# {{lb|en|two-up}} The piece of wood on which the [[spinner]] places the coins and then uses for throwing them.<ref>Sidney J. Baker, ''The Australian Language'', second edition, 1966, chapter XI section 3, page 242</ref>
#: {{syn|en|kip|kylie|lannet|stick}}
# {{lb|en|mining}} [[shale|Shale]] or [[bituminous]] shale.
#* {{quote-text|en|year=1799|author=w:Richard Kirwan|title=Geological Essays
|passage=bituminous shale ; which miners , if I mistake not , call '''bat'''}}
# A [[sheet]] of [[cotton]] used for filling [[quilt]]s or [[comfortable]]s; [[batting]].
# A part of a [[brick]] with one whole end. <!--see brickbat-->
# A [[stroke]]; a [[sharp]] [[blow]].
# {{lb|en|pottery}} A removable flat board or disk attached to a [[potter's wheel]] prior to [[throwing]] used to transport and dry [[greenware]].
# {{lb|en|UK|Scotland|dialect}} A stroke of work.
# {{lb|en|informal}} Rate of motion; speed.
#* {{quote-text|en|year=1842|title=Sporting Magazine|page=251
|passage=On starting, The Nun led at a very slow pace for a quarter of a mile, when the Shrigley colt made running at a good '''bat'''.}}
#* {{quote-text|en|year=1898|author=unknown author|title=Pall Mall Magazine
|passage=a vast host of fowl {{...}} making at full '''bat''' for the North Sea.}}
# {{lb|en|US|slang|dated}} A [[spree]]; a [[jollification]]; a [[binge]], [[jag]].
# {{lb|en|UK|Scotland|dialect}} Manner; rate; condition; state of health.

===Etymology 3===
{{etymid|en|to hit}}
From {{inh|en|enm|baten|batten}}, {{m|enm|baten|t=to beat|id=to beat}}, from {{der|en|fro|batre||to beat}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|batto|battere}}, from {{der|en|la|battuo|battuere}}, of {{unc|en|title=uncertain}} origin; perhaps of {{der|en|gem|-}} or {{der|en|cel|-}} origin. In modern English reinterpreted as a verbal derivative of Etymology 2. Compare {{m|en|batter}}, {{m|en|battery}}.

====Verb====
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To hit with a bat or (figuratively) as if with a bat.
#: {{ux|en|He '''batted''' the ball away with a satisfying thwack.}}
#: {{ux|en|We '''batted''' a few ideas around.}}
# {{senseid|en|take a turn at hitting}}{{lb|en|intransitive}} To take a turn at hitting a ball with a bat in sports like [[cricket]], [[baseball]] and [[softball]], as opposed to [[field]]ing.
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[strike]] or [[swipe]] as though with a bat.
#: {{ux|en|The cat '''batted''' at the toy.}}
# {{lb|en|UK|dialect|obsolete}} To [[bate]] or flutter, as a [[hawk]].

====Usage notes====
* To prepare a bed (in the sense of sleeping furniture) is usually to {{m|en|make the bed}}, or {{qualifier|Southern US}} to {{m|en|spread the bed}}, the verb {{m|en|spread}} probably having been developed from {{m|en|bedspread}}. Like many nouns denoting places where people spend time, {{m|en||bed}} requires no article after certain prepositions: hence {{m|en||in bed|lying in a bed}}, {{m|en||go to bed|get into a bed}}, and so on. The forms {{m|en||in a bed}}, etc. do exist, but tend to imply mere presence in the bed, without it being for the purpose of sleep.
